books.title: The Lean Startup
books.author: Eric Ries
books.description: How to build companies under extreme uncertainty by learning fast from real customers.
ideas: Build, measure, learn

Most failed startups don't fail because they couldn't build their product; they fail because they built something nobody wanted. Eric Ries suggests treating every product idea as an experiment. Build the smallest version that tests your assumption, measure how real people actually behave and learn whether to continue or change direction. Then repeat, faster each time. The goal is to shorten the loop from idea to evidence. Today: write down one assumption about your project, such as "people will pay for this", and think of the cheapest way to test it this week.
The minimum viable product

A minimum viable product isn't a cheap version of your dream; it's the quickest way to start learning. Sometimes it's not even a real product. Dropbox famously tested demand with a simple video showing how the service would work, before building most of it. Others have run a service by hand behind a website to see if customers would use it. Today: imagine the simplest possible version of your idea that would tell you whether people want it, and sketch how you could build it in a week.
Pivot or persevere

At regular points, Ries recommends an honest meeting with a hard question: is this working, or should we change a fundamental part of the strategy? A pivot keeps what you've learned but changes direction, such as a new customer, feature or business model. Many famous companies, from YouTube to Slack, pivoted from very different starting ideas. Persevering blindly wastes years; pivoting too often wastes focus. Today: set a date to review a project you're working on, and decide in advance what evidence would make you change course.
Vanity metrics

Total sign-ups, page views and downloads feel great on a dashboard, but they can rise while a business quietly fails. Ries calls them vanity metrics. More useful are numbers that reflect real behaviour: how many users come back next week, how many pay, how many recommend you. Good metrics help you make decisions; vanity metrics just make you feel good. Today: look at the numbers you track for a project or goal, and ask which ones actually change what you'd do next.
Validated learning

In a startup, progress isn't measured by lines of code written or features shipped. It's measured by what you've learned about customers, backed by evidence. Ries calls this validated learning. A week that proves an idea wrong is a productive week, because it saves months of building in the wrong direction. Today: at the end of your week, write down one thing you've genuinely learned about your customers or audience, not just what you've done.

books.title: Zero to One
books.author: Peter Thiel & Blake Masters
books.description: Notes on startups and how to build companies that create something genuinely new.
ideas: Zero to one versus one to n

Copying what already works, opening another café or launching another similar app, takes the world from one to n: more of the same. Creating something genuinely new takes it from zero to one. Peter Thiel argues that the biggest value comes from the latter, because new things can't be competed away easily. Not every project needs to be revolutionary, but it's worth asking whether you're adding something new or just more. Today: think about your work and ask what you're doing that no one else is.
The contrarian question

Thiel likes to ask job candidates a hard question: what important truth do very few people agree with you on? It's difficult because it requires both original thinking and the courage to say something unpopular. Great businesses are often built on such secrets, like insights others have missed or dismissed. Today: spend ten minutes trying to answer Thiel's question for yourself. Even if you don't find an answer, the search sharpens your thinking.
Start small and monopolize

Starting by competing in a huge, crowded market is a fast way to make no profit. Thiel recommends dominating a small, specific market first, then expanding. Amazon began with books; Facebook began at a single university. Owning a niche gives you a base of loyal customers, cash and lessons before you take on bigger challenges. Today: if you're building something, define the smallest group of people you could serve brilliantly, and focus on them.
Competition erodes profit

In perfect competition, where many similar firms sell the same thing, profits get competed down to almost nothing. Thiel argues that lasting businesses have something unique that protects them, such as proprietary technology, strong network effects, economies of scale or a powerful brand. Competition feels virtuous, but it often traps companies in a race to the bottom. Today: ask what makes your work hard to copy, and how you could make that advantage stronger.

books.title: Good to Great
books.author: Jim Collins
books.description: A research study into why some companies make the leap to lasting greatness and others don't.
ideas: First who, then what

Jim Collins studied companies that went from good to truly great and found that their leaders first got the right people on the bus, and the wrong people off, before deciding where to drive it. With the right people, the direction becomes easier to choose and to change. With the wrong people, even a brilliant strategy fails. Today: think about a team you're part of and ask who you'd want with you on any journey, regardless of the destination.
Level 5 leadership

The leaders behind the great companies in Collins' study surprised him. They weren't flashy, celebrity CEOs. They combined deep personal humility with intense professional will. They gave credit to others when things went well and took responsibility when things went badly. Collins called this Level 5 leadership. Today: notice how you talk about successes and failures. Try crediting others for one win and owning one setback yourself.
The hedgehog concept

Collins describes the hedgehog concept: the intersection of three circles. What can you be the best in the world at? What drives your economic engine? What are you deeply passionate about? Great companies focused relentlessly on where those circles overlapped, ignoring tempting distractions. Individuals can use the same lens for careers. Today: draw three circles and fill them in for yourself. Where do they overlap?
The flywheel

Great companies rarely transform in one dramatic moment. Collins compares their progress to pushing a giant, heavy flywheel. At first it barely moves, but consistent pushes in the same direction build momentum until it spins on its own. From the outside it looks like a sudden breakthrough; from the inside it was years of steady effort. Today: identify one consistent push you can make toward a goal every day this week, and keep pushing even if nothing seems to move.
Confront the brutal facts

The great companies in Collins' study shared a paradox: they kept unwavering faith that they would succeed in the end, while honestly confronting the harshest facts of their current reality. He named this the Stockdale Paradox after a prisoner of war who survived years of captivity. Optimism without honesty leads to disappointment; honesty without faith leads to despair. Today: face one uncomfortable fact about a goal of yours, and remind yourself why you'll still get there.

books.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
books.author: Clayton M. Christensen
books.description: Why well-run companies can do everything right and still be overtaken by new technologies.
ideas: Disruptive innovation

Clayton Christensen noticed a strange pattern: well-run companies, doing everything right, were often overtaken by newcomers with simpler, cheaper products. These disruptors start with customers the big players ignore, people who don't need the best and most expensive option, then steadily improve until they challenge the main market. Digital cameras, cheap steel and budget airlines followed this path. Today: think about your industry and ask what simpler, cheaper alternative might be quietly improving at the edges.
Listening to customers can mislead

Big companies listen carefully to their best customers, who ask for more features and higher performance. That sounds smart, but Christensen showed it can be a trap. It pushes companies upmarket, leaving the low end open to newcomers with "good enough" products. By the time the threat is obvious, it's too late. Today: ask whether you're only listening to your most demanding customers, and what you might be missing from those who want something simpler.
Small markets don't excite big companies

A new market worth a few million pounds is exciting for a startup but meaningless to a giant company with billions in revenue. So big firms often ignore emerging opportunities until they're too large to catch. Christensen called this one of the core reasons incumbents fail. Today: look at a small, unglamorous opportunity you've been dismissing, and ask what it might become in ten years.
Create a separate unit

Christensen found that incumbents who successfully handled disruption often did it by creating a separate unit, with its own goals, cost structure and culture, free from the pressures of the main business. Inside the main company, the new idea would be judged by the wrong standards and starved of resources. Today: if you're trying something new within an established structure, ask whether it needs its own space and rules to grow.

books.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
books.author: Ben Horowitz
books.description: A frank guide to the problems no business book prepares you for, from layoffs to near-bankruptcy.
ideas: There's no recipe

Management books often describe how to avoid problems. Ben Horowitz, a venture capitalist and former CEO, writes about the hard things: situations with no clean answer, like laying off friends, firing an executive or deciding whether to sell the company. In those moments, there's no recipe; you have to choose the least bad option and live with it. Today: if you're facing a hard decision, accept that there may be no perfect answer, and choose the option you could explain honestly to everyone affected.
The struggle

Every founder, Horowitz writes, goes through the struggle: periods when nothing works, the money is running out and quitting looks like the sensible choice. He describes it as feeling alone and doubting everything. But going through the struggle is part of building anything worthwhile, not a sign of failure. Many great companies nearly died several times. Today: if you're in a tough stretch, remind yourself it's a normal part of the path, and focus on the next small step.
Take care of people, products and profits, in that order

Horowitz insists on an order of priorities: take care of the people, then the products, then the profits. Without good people who feel valued, you can't build great products; without great products, profits won't last. It sounds simple, but under pressure many leaders reverse the order. Today: think of one way you could make the people you work with feel more supported, and act on it.
Tell it like it is

When things go badly, the temptation is to hide the bad news to avoid panic. Horowitz argues the opposite: tell it like it is. Being honest with your team about problems builds trust and lets everyone help solve them. Hiding bad news makes the hard thing harder, because people sense something is wrong and fill the silence with worse stories. Today: share one piece of honest, difficult news with the people it affects, along with your plan to deal with it.

books.title: Rework
books.author: Jason Fried & David Heinemeier Hansson
books.description: Short essays challenging conventional business wisdom about growth, planning and work.
ideas: Planning is guessing

Long-term business plans pretend you can predict the future, but markets, customers and technology change constantly. Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson call planning a form of guessing. Instead of writing a five-year plan, decide what you'll do this week, do it, then adjust based on what you learn. It's less stressful and more realistic. Today: replace one long-range plan with a clear decision about what you'll do in the next seven days.
Small is fine

Not every company needs to become huge. The founders of Basecamp argue that staying small and profitable can bring more freedom, less stress and better products than chasing growth at any cost. Small teams make decisions faster, waste less and stay close to customers. Growth should be a choice, not an obligation. Today: think about one area of your life or work where "bigger" isn't actually better, and enjoy keeping it small.
Build half a product, not a half-assed product

When time or money is short, the authors advise cutting features ruthlessly and doing what's left really well. Half a product that works beautifully is better than a full product that works badly. This forces you to decide what truly matters to your customers. Today: look at a project you're working on and identify one feature or task you could drop to make the rest better.
Meetings are toxic

A one-hour meeting with ten people isn't one hour; it's ten hours of work time gone. Fried and Heinemeier Hansson call most meetings toxic: they interrupt focus, drift off topic and rarely produce clear decisions. When you must meet, keep it small, short, with a clear agenda and a clear end. Today: cancel or shorten one meeting this week, or replace it with a short written update.
Say no by default

Every yes adds complexity: another feature to maintain, another commitment to keep. The authors recommend saying no by default, even to good ideas, so the product stays simple and focused. The truly important requests will come back again and again. Today: practise saying no to one request that doesn't fit your priorities, politely and without long explanations.

books.title: Shape Up
books.author: Ryan Singer
books.description: How Basecamp plans and builds software in six-week cycles without endless backlogs.

free.note: Free to read on the publisher's site. All rights reserved, so it's read there, not copied into the app.

ideas: Fixed time, variable scope

Most teams estimate how long a feature will take and then watch the estimate slip. Ryan Singer describes a different approach used at Basecamp: decide how much time a problem is worth, its appetite, and shape the solution to fit that time. A two-week appetite produces a different solution than a six-week one. Fixed time, variable scope keeps projects from dragging on forever. Today: for your next task, decide in advance how much time it deserves, and design your approach to fit.
Shape before you build

Before handing work to a team, senior people at Basecamp shape it: they define the problem, sketch a rough solution and identify risks, at just the right level of detail. Too vague, and the team flounders; too detailed, and there's no room for their creativity. Shaping is like giving someone a map with landmarks, not turn-by-turn directions. Today: when you delegate a task, describe the problem, the boundaries and the rough shape of a solution, then let them fill in the details.
Bets, not backlogs

Instead of an ever-growing backlog of ideas, leaders review a few shaped pitches each cycle and bet on the ones worth doing. Unchosen ideas aren't kept in a guilt-inducing list; if they're important, they'll come up again. This keeps teams focused and decisions clear. Today: look at your own to-do list or backlog and delete or archive anything you haven't touched in months. If it matters, it will return.
Six-week cycles and cool-down

Basecamp teams work uninterrupted for six weeks, long enough to build something meaningful, short enough to keep urgency. Then they take two weeks of cool-down to fix bugs, explore ideas and breathe. The rhythm protects focus and prevents burnout. Today: try your own version: pick a focused period for a project, followed by a short break to reflect before starting the next one.
Hill charts

Work, Singer explains, has an uphill phase where you're figuring things out and solving unknowns, and a downhill phase where you're simply executing. Basecamp teams use hill charts to show where each piece of work sits, which reveals real progress far better than counting completed tasks. A task stuck uphill for too long is a warning sign. Today: look at a project you're working on and ask which parts are still uphill, full of unknowns, and tackle one of those first.

books.title: Getting Real
books.author: 37signals
books.description: The small, fast, less-is-more approach to building web software that 37signals used to make Basecamp.

free.note: Free to read on the publisher's site. All rights reserved, so it's read there, not copied into the app.

ideas: Build less

Basecamp's founders built their product by doing less than their competitors on purpose. Fewer features meant less to maintain, a simpler product and a clearer message. Many customers actually preferred the simpler option. Building less isn't laziness; it's discipline about what really matters. Today: look at something you're making and ask what you could remove to make it better.
Embrace constraints

Limited time, money and people force focus and creativity. Instead of complaining about constraints, the authors argue, embrace them. A small budget makes you find clever solutions; a tight deadline forces you to cut the unnecessary. Some of the best products were created by tiny teams with very little. Today: think of one constraint you're facing and ask how it could push you toward a simpler, better solution.
Start with the interface

Many software projects start with databases and code, then bolt on the screens at the end. Getting Real suggests the opposite: design the interface people will actually use first. It's much cheaper to change a sketch than a finished system, and it keeps the focus on the user's experience. Today: before starting a project, sketch what the end result will look like for the person using it.
Launch, then iterate

Real usage teaches far more than plans and predictions. The authors recommend getting a simple version out into the world, listening carefully to customers and improving in small steps. Waiting for perfection delays learning. Many successful products launched rough and improved quickly. Today: take something you've been polishing and share an early version with a few real users this week.
Say no by default

Every feature request sounds reasonable on its own. Say yes to all of them, and your product becomes a cluttered mess. The authors suggest saying no by default and listening for the requests that keep coming back. Those are the ones worth considering. Saying no keeps the product coherent and the team focused. Today: when someone asks for something extra on a project, practise a polite "not now", and note it down to see whether it comes up again.
